title: The Mathematical Modeling Software Database — Overview: software that does mathematics
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. Mathematical modeling software turns equations into answers: symbolic systems manipulate formulas exactly, numeric systems approximate solutions to any precision, and statistical systems learn from data. MATLAB grew from matrix laboratory into engineering's workbench; Mathematica made symbolic computation mainstream; Maple serves classrooms and engineers; GNU Octave offers a free MATLAB-compatible language; SageMath unites open-source mathematics; Julia was built for speed in scientific computing; R rules statistics. Each record carries a working demo in the tool's spirit, runnable here.
capabilities: Symbolic, numeric, and statistical modeling compared
Seven real tools with honest capability records
How to choose: problem-first tool selection

title: The Mathematical Modeling Software Database — MATLAB
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. MATLAB, from MathWorks (first released 1984), is the matrix laboratory: everything is an array, and linear algebra is the native tongue. Engineers model control systems, signal processing chains, and image pipelines in it; Simulink extends it to block-diagram simulation. It is commercial software with academic licensing, running on Windows, macOS, and Linux. The demo below works in MATLAB's spirit — matrix multiplication, the operation the whole environment is named for.
capabilities: Everything is an array; linear algebra as native tongue

title: The Mathematical Modeling Software Database — Wolfram Mathematica
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. Wolfram Mathematica (1988) made symbolic computation mainstream: it differentiates, integrates, and solves equations exactly, keeping pi as pi instead of 3.14159 until you ask for digits. Its Wolfram Language is a vast functional programming environment spanning mathematics, visualization, and knowledge queries. Commercial software from Wolfram Research, it runs on desktop platforms and in the cloud. The demo shows symbolic-style simplification the way Mathematica thinks — exact before numeric.
capabilities: Exact mathematics: pi stays pi until digits are requested
The Wolfram Language: functional and vast

title: The Mathematical Modeling Software Database — Maple
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. Maple, from Maplesoft (a University of Waterloo spin-off), is a symbolic and numeric computation environment beloved in classrooms and engineering firms. It solves differential equations analytically where possible, renders mathematics in natural notation, and documents computations as live worksheets mixing text, math, and code. Commercial software with strong education pricing, it competes directly with Mathematica in the symbolic space. The demo finds roots numerically, the way Maple falls back when closed forms run out.
capabilities: Natural math notation and live worksheets
Numeric fallback when closed forms run out

title: The Mathematical Modeling Software Database — GNU Octave
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. GNU Octave is the free-software answer to MATLAB: a high-level language for numerical computation that runs most MATLAB scripts unchanged. Maintained by the GNU project, it covers matrices, plotting, signal processing, and optimization without license fees, making it the classroom and startup choice where budgets are thin. It runs on Windows, macOS, and Linux. The demo solves a linear system by elimination — the bread and butter of numerical modeling.

title: The Mathematical Modeling Software Database — SageMath
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. SageMath is an open-source mathematics system that unites many free packages — NumPy, SymPy, Maxima, R, and more — under one Python-based interface. It aims to be a viable free alternative to the commercial symbolic systems, covering algebra, calculus, number theory, and combinatorics. The demo tests primality the way a number-theory session in Sage would begin: asking which numbers are prime.
capabilities: Unites NumPy, SymPy, Maxima, R under one roof
The free alternative to commercial symbolic systems

title: The Mathematical Modeling Software Database — Julia
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. Julia (first released 2012) was designed to solve the two-language problem: researchers prototype in a slow friendly language, then rewrite in a fast painful one. Julia's just-in-time compilation runs loops at near-C speed while keeping readable math-like syntax, and its multiple dispatch makes generic numerical code natural. Free and open source, it shines in scientific computing, differential equations (DifferentialEquations.jl), and optimization. The demo shows vectorized-style computation at speed.
capabilities: Multiple dispatch for generic numerical code

title: The Mathematical Modeling Software Database — R for statistics
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. R is the lingua franca of statistics: born from S at the University of Auckland, it is the environment where new statistical methods are published first. Data frames, formulas like y ~ x, and a vast CRAN package archive make it the default for data analysis, biostatistics, and visualization (ggplot2). Free and open source, it trades raw speed for expressiveness in analysis. The demo computes the descriptive statistics every R session starts with: mean and standard deviation.
capabilities: The lingua franca of statistics, from S
Data frames, model formulas, and CRAN packages
